title: What is the difference between eager watermarks (minimize latency, may miss late events) and relaxed watermarks (higher accuracy, increased latency), and how do you choose based on your use case?
shortTitle: Eager vs relaxed watermarks in Flink

s1_definition.profdef: Eager and relaxed watermarks describe two ends of a tuning spectrum for the out-of-orderness bound in a watermark strategy. An eager watermark uses a small or zero out-of-orderness delay so the watermark advances quickly and closely tracks the maximum observed event time, which minimizes window latency but treats more slightly-delayed events as late. A relaxed watermark uses a larger out-of-orderness delay so the watermark trails further behind the maximum observed time, which waits longer for stragglers and therefore captures more late events at the cost of higher latency. The choice is a direct latency-versus-completeness decision driven by how late your data realistically arrives and how much accuracy your use case demands.
s1_definition.analogy: The National Bank of India must decide how long to hold a business minute open before declaring it closed and publishing the total. An eager policy is an impatient manager who closes the minute the instant the clock ticks over, so the report comes out fast, but any transaction slip still walking through the door a few seconds late is thrown away. A relaxed policy is a patient manager who holds the minute open for an extra ten seconds to let stragglers arrive, so the total is more accurate but the report is published later. Neither is universally right; a fraud alert wants the impatient manager for speed, while an end-of-day settlement total wants the patient manager for accuracy.
s1_definition.oneliner: Eager watermarks fire fast but drop more stragglers, relaxed watermarks wait longer but capture them, and you choose based on whether speed or completeness matters more.
s1_definition.raw:
**Professional definition:** Eager and relaxed watermarks describe two ends of a tuning spectrum for the out-of-orderness bound in a watermark strategy. An eager watermark uses a small or zero out-of-orderness delay so the watermark advances quickly and closely tracks the maximum observed event time, which minimizes window latency but treats more slightly-delayed events as late. A relaxed watermark uses a larger out-of-orderness delay so the watermark trails further behind the maximum observed time, which waits longer for stragglers and therefore captures more late events at the cost of higher latency. The choice is a direct latency-versus-completeness decision driven by how late your data realistically arrives and how much accuracy your use case demands.

**In simple words (banking analogy):** The National Bank of India must decide how long to hold a business minute open before declaring it closed and publishing the total. An eager policy is an impatient manager who closes the minute the instant the clock ticks over, so the report comes out fast, but any transaction slip still walking through the door a few seconds late is thrown away. A relaxed policy is a patient manager who holds the minute open for an extra ten seconds to let stragglers arrive, so the total is more accurate but the report is published later. Neither is universally right; a fraud alert wants the impatient manager for speed, while an end-of-day settlement total wants the patient manager for accuracy.

**One line to remember:** Eager watermarks fire fast but drop more stragglers, relaxed watermarks wait longer but capture them, and you choose based on whether speed or completeness matters more.

sections.s2_technical:
Both eager and relaxed watermarks typically use the same bounded-out-of-orderness strategy; the difference is purely the delay value. An eager configuration is `WatermarkStrategy.forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofMillis(200))` or even `forMonotonousTimestamps()` which assumes zero out-of-orderness. Because the watermark sits very close to the latest event time, the watermark crosses each window's end almost immediately after the last expected event, so the window fires with very low latency. The downside is that any event that is even slightly out of order relative to that tight bound arrives after the watermark has passed and is treated as late, so with no allowed lateness it is dropped, producing an incomplete result.

A relaxed configuration is something like `forBoundedOutOfOrderness(Duration.ofSeconds(30))`. The watermark trails thirty seconds behind the maximum observed timestamp, so each window waits an extra thirty seconds of event time before firing. This captures almost all realistically late events, giving a much more complete and accurate result, but every downstream result is delayed by that extra waiting time and more windows stay open in memory simultaneously. 

The right way to choose is to measure the lateness distribution of your actual source and then match the watermark to the use case rather than guessing. For a low-latency alerting pipeline where reacting in a second matters more than perfect counts, you lean eager and accept that a tiny fraction of stragglers are missed. For an auditable or financial aggregate where the number must be right, you lean relaxed so the window waits for stragglers. A powerful middle path is to combine an eager watermark with allowed lateness and a side output: the window fires eagerly for low latency, then re-emits corrected results as late events trickle in within the allowed lateness, and the extreme tail goes to a side output. This gives speculative speed and eventual accuracy at the same time. The senior nuance is that watermark delay is a global latency tax on every window, so you should not inflate it just to catch a rare straggler; it is usually better to keep the watermark reasonably eager and use allowed lateness for correction, because that only pays the extra cost for the windows that actually receive late data.
sections.s3_banking:
Problem 1 — The National Bank of India runs a real-time fraud alert that counts transactions per account per ten-second window. Speed is everything: if a card is being tested, the bank wants to react within a second or two, and missing one straggler transaction out of hundreds barely changes the alert decision. This is exactly the case for an eager watermark with almost no out-of-orderness delay, so windows fire fast even if a few late transactions are dropped.

Problem 2 — The same bank also runs an end-of-day interest and settlement aggregate over the same transactions, and here the number must be exactly right because it feeds the general ledger and regulatory reporting. Missing even one straggler transaction would make the ledger not balance. This is exactly the case for a relaxed watermark with a generous out-of-orderness delay, so every window waits long enough to capture all realistically late transactions before it fires.

In the mini-project we build a runnable demo that processes the same out-of-order stream twice, once with an eager watermark and once with a relaxed watermark, and compares how many transactions each path counts. We define a `Movement` record with an event time and amount. A `WatermarkPolicy` holds an out-of-orderness delay and computes the watermark. A `WindowAggregator` buckets movements into ten-second windows and, when a window's end is passed by the watermark, fires it, dropping any movement that arrives after its window has fired. A `EagerVsRelaxedDemo` main class feeds a stream with a couple of genuinely late movements and runs it under an eager policy and a relaxed policy, printing the per-window counts and totals so the reader sees the eager path miss stragglers while the relaxed path captures them.

```yaml
# application.yml
flink:
  eager-relaxed:
    window-seconds: 10
    eager-ooo-millis: 200      # eager: fire fast
    relaxed-ooo-millis: 30000  # relaxed: wait for stragglers
```

sections.s5_journey:
Input data: five movements for Rajesh (SAV2001) with event times 1 second, 3 seconds, 12 seconds, 5 seconds, and 20 seconds, with a ten-second window. The movement at 5 seconds arrives after the one at 12 seconds, making it a straggler for the window from 0 to 10 seconds.

Step 1, Eager run with 200 millisecond delay: Movements at 1 and 3 seconds enter the 0-to-10 window. The max seen is 3 seconds, watermark 2.8 seconds, below the window end of 10 seconds, so nothing fires yet.

Step 2, Eager continues: The movement at 12 seconds arrives. Max seen jumps to 12 seconds, watermark becomes 11.8 seconds, which is past the 0-to-10 window end of 10 seconds. The 0-to-10 window fires with count two and total 300.

Step 3, Eager straggler: The movement at 5 seconds arrives. Its window is 0-to-10, whose end is 10 seconds, but the watermark is already 11.8 seconds. The window has fired, so this straggler is dropped. The eager path loses 400 rupees of real money from the window count.

Step 4, Relaxed run with 30 second delay: Movements at 1, 3, and 12 seconds arrive. With a thirty-second delay the watermark stays far behind: after 12 seconds the max seen is 12 and the watermark is 12 minus 30, which is negative, so no window fires yet and the 0-to-10 window stays open.

Step 5, Relaxed straggler: The movement at 5 seconds arrives while the 0-to-10 window is still open, so it is accepted into that window, bringing its count to three and total to 700. The relaxed path captured the straggler that the eager path dropped.

Step 6, Relaxed firing: The movement at 20 seconds advances the max seen to 20 seconds, but the watermark is 20 minus 30, still negative, so the window only fires much later once the watermark finally crosses 10 seconds. The relaxed path is accurate but publishes later, exactly the latency-versus-completeness tradeoff, and it dropped zero stragglers.

Final output:

```
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] === EAGER watermark (ooo=200ms) ===
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] FIRE window=0 count=2 total=300
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [WARNING] DROPPED late movement SAV2001 ts=5000 window=0
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Dropped stragglers = 1
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] === RELAXED watermark (ooo=30000ms) ===
2026-10-30 07:41:00 [INFO] Dropped stragglers = 0
```

sections.s6_takeaway:
Eager and relaxed watermarks are two ends of a single tuning spectrum, and the dial between them is the out-of-orderness bound in the watermark strategy. An eager watermark uses a very small or zero out-of-orderness delay, so the watermark hugs the maximum observed event time and crosses each window's end almost immediately after the last expected event. That gives the lowest possible latency because windows fire fast, but it treats any even slightly-delayed event as late, so with no allowed lateness those stragglers are dropped and the result can be incomplete. A relaxed watermark uses a larger delay, so the watermark trails well behind the latest event time and each window waits longer before firing. That captures almost all realistically late events and gives an accurate, complete result, but every downstream result is delayed by that extra waiting and more windows sit open in memory.

How you choose comes down to what the use case values. If you are doing real-time alerting where reacting in a second matters far more than perfect counts, you lean eager and accept missing a rare straggler. If you are producing an auditable or financial aggregate where the number must be exactly right, you lean relaxed so the window waits for every straggler. The most powerful approach in practice is a hybrid: keep the watermark fairly eager for low latency, but add allowed lateness so the window re-emits corrected results as late events trickle in, with a side output for the extreme tail. That way you pay the extra waiting cost only on the windows that actually receive late data, instead of taxing every window with a large watermark delay. And you never pick the delay by guessing; you measure the real lateness distribution of the source and set the bound to cover the bulk of it.

At the National Bank of India I ran exactly these two profiles over the same transaction stream. The fraud alerting job used an eager watermark of a couple hundred milliseconds so it could flag a card-testing burst within a second or two, and missing one straggler out of hundreds did not change the alert. The end-of-day settlement job, feeding the general ledger and regulatory reports, used a relaxed watermark of about thirty seconds because the totals had to balance to the rupee and we could not afford to drop even one late transaction. I could show concretely that the eager path dropped a straggler and undercounted a window while the relaxed path captured it and was complete but published later. Being able to articulate that the watermark delay is a global latency tax, and that the smart move is often an eager watermark plus allowed lateness rather than a blanket large delay, is the kind of reasoning that signals real production experience.
